opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at something fundamental about where agents are today versus where people imagine them to be.

If you look at what coding agents are really good at, it's writing glue code, calling libraries, refactoring, fixing bugs. But predictive modeling on real enterprise data is a very different beast. The data doesn't live in one nice CSV file. It lives in a relational database with dozens or hundreds of tables: customers, transactions, products, support tickets, all connected through primary and foreign keys. And the traditional workflow for building a model on top of that is incredibly manual. You have to figure out which tables matter, write the joins, do the aggregations, engineer hundreds of features, worry about time leakage, build training tables, pick a model, tune it, and so on. That's weeks or months of a data scientist's time, and it's full of subtle decisions where, if you get one wrong, you get a model that looks great offline and fails in production.

So if you hand that whole process to a coding agent operating at the level of pandas and scikit-learn, you're asking it to reproduce all that tacit expertise line by line. It can generate a lot of code, but the search space is huge, and the failure modes are quiet. Leakage doesn't throw an exception. A bad feature doesn't crash. The agent can confidently produce something that's wrong, and it's very hard for it, or for the human, to tell.

What we've been arguing is that the right abstraction is to let the agent express the predictive question declaratively, something like "for each customer, what's the probability they churn in the next 30 days," and then have a foundation model that operates directly on the relational data answer it. That's what relational deep learning and relational foundation models give you: the model learns over the graph of the database itself, so you don't need hand-crafted feature engineering. Then the agent's job becomes reasoning about the business problem: what to predict, for which entities, over what time horizon, how to evaluate it, rather than reinventing the plumbing every time.

It's a bit like the shift from assembly to SQL. SQL didn't make programmers obsolete; it let them think about what they want from the data instead of how to physically retrieve it. I think predictive modeling needs that same kind of query language, and once you have it, agents become dramatically more effective, because now they're operating at the level where their reasoning is actually strong, and the heavy, error-prone numerical work is handled by a model that's been built for exactly that.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot. If you look at what coding agents are actually good at today, they're great at manipulating code that operates on text and on files. But predictive modeling over enterprise data is a fundamentally different kind of problem. You have data sitting in a relational database, dozens of tables, foreign keys, time stamps, and the question is something like, which customers are going to churn next month, or which transactions are fraudulent, or what will demand look like for this product.

If you ask a coding agent to solve that with the primitives it has today, it has to do the whole thing by hand. It has to figure out which tables matter, write the joins, decide how far back in time to aggregate, build features, make sure it doesn't leak information from the future into the training set, pick a model, tune it, and then stitch all of that together. That's thousands of lines of pandas and SQL and scikit-learn, and every one of those steps is a place where it can make a subtle mistake. And the worst part is the mistakes aren't syntax errors. The code runs. It just quietly gives you a model that's wrong, and neither the agent nor the user can easily tell.

So our view is that the agent needs a layer of abstraction that matches the level at which the task is actually specified. The human says, predict churn for these customers over the next thirty days. The agent should be able to express essentially that same intent to a system that understands relational data natively, something like a predictive query, where the heavy lifting of walking the schema, handling time, and learning the representation is done underneath by a model that was built for that. That's really what we've been doing with relational foundation models, treating the whole database as the input rather than making someone hand-engineer a flat table.

There's a nice analogy to how we got here with software in general. Nobody wants an agent writing assembly. You give it high-level languages and libraries so that the space of things it can get wrong shrinks and the things it does get right compose. Predictive modeling needs that same move. When the API is at the right level, the agent spends its reasoning on the question, what should we predict and how does it fit into the workflow, instead of on whether it remembered to filter by the right date column. And then, honestly, the results are better and they're a lot more trustworthy, because the correctness is baked into the system rather than reinvented every time.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that predictive modeling is not just about writing code. You have to decide what you’re predicting, what information is available at prediction time, how to construct the training examples, and how to evaluate the result. An agent can produce code that runs perfectly and still solve the wrong problem—or accidentally use information from the future.

Higher-level APIs give the agent a way to express those decisions without having to rebuild all the underlying machinery. For example, it could specify, “Predict which customers will make a purchase in the next thirty days,” and use an interface that handles the data preparation, training, and evaluation with consistent time boundaries.

That lets the agent focus on the task definition and on interpreting the results. It also makes its work easier to check. Instead of inspecting thousands of lines of generated code, you can examine a smaller set of explicit modeling choices. So the value is both efficiency and reliability: you’re giving the agent abstractions that match the problem it’s trying to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
If you give a coding agent only low-level tools, it has to reinvent the entire predictive modeling pipeline. It has to figure out how to join the tables, construct features, avoid leaking future information, train a model, and evaluate it correctly. There are many opportunities to produce code that runs but answers the wrong question.

A higher-level API lets the agent operate closer to the intent: predict which customers will churn, for example, using the information available at a particular point in time. The underlying system can handle the mechanics of learning from the database, while the agent focuses on defining the prediction task and interpreting the result.

That separation is important. We don’t expect a coding agent to implement a database engine every time it needs to query data. Similarly, it should be able to invoke a reliable predictive modeling capability without rebuilding all of machine learning from scratch.
